# Agents {#sec-agents}

<!-- this chapter sits between the chatbot and tool calling chapter (see function_calling.qmd) and the multi-agents chapter (llm_pipelines.qmd) (rag was also introduced before). it reiterates tool calling and introduces agents (basically as a loop around a tool call). we introduce googles adk as the main framework used in this course, other frameworks are mentioned as well. students build their first agent with adk. tools are reiterated again, this time in the form of anthropics model context protocol. students should connect to an app using mcp -->


## Introduction

So far in this course we covered the fundamentals of language models. We talked about chatbots and built the harness behind tool calling — a way for the model to request an action and have it actually carried out. We also covered retrieval augmented generation (RAG) in some detail.

Today, we move one step further: we look at systems in which an LLM controls the flow of an application, orchestrates tools, and decides which steps to take next. These systems are often called agents. Closely related are LLM pipelines, where we hard-code a sequence of steps instead of letting the model decide dynamically.

A concrete picture of what that control looks like: in *Vending-Bench* [@backlundVendingBenchBenchmarkLongTerm2025], an LLM agent runs a simulated vending-machine business end to end — deciding what to stock, when to restock, and which prices to set — based on its own read of demand and competition, with nobody hard-coding the order of those decisions. It's also a good showcase of how and why such systems fail once nobody is steering turn by turn.


## A Closer Look at Tools

Before we get there, let's take a closer look at tools — because tools are what give an LLM the ability to actually *do* things, rather than just talk about them.

We can broadly distinguish two kinds of tools. The first kind is **read-only and non-invasive**: the model can observe the world, but not change it. Examples include reading files, searching a vector store, or running a quick web search.

The second kind involves **actions** — tools that change state in the world. This includes sending emails; writing, modifying, or deleting files; executing commands, scripts, or code; opening and interacting with other applications; or installing additional software. And, at the more adventurous end of the spectrum: ordering things online, investing in totally valid cryptocurrency schemes, deleting all your files, or corrupting your operating system.

The distinction matters, because read-only tools are relatively safe to hand to an autonomous system — the worst case is a bad answer. Action tools, by contrast, can have real, irreversible consequences. 

As discussed in @sec-functioncalling, integrating a tool requires the following steps:

1. The LLM must know which tools are available — typically via descriptions passed in the system prompt.
2. The LLM must be instructed to produce its response in a structured format when it intends to call a tool.
3. That response must be parsed to extract the tool call and its arguments.
4. Finally, the tool must actually be executed, and the result fed back to the model.

With this infrastructure in place, we are only one small step away from an agent.


## Agents: closing the loop

Once tool calling and execution are in place, building an agent is conceptually straightforward: it is essentially a loop wrapped around the tool-calling mechanism.

![Image credit https://x.com/adamdotdev (from [the Tiny Agents blogpost](https://huggingface.co/blog/tiny-agents))](../imgs/agent_loop_tinyagents.jpg)

One of the earliest and most influential patterns for structuring this loop is _ReAct_ (Reasoning + Acting), introduced by Yao et al. [@yaoReActSynergizingReasoning2023]. Many current agents don't spell out explicit "Thought:"/"Action:" text anymore — native tool-calling APIs and reasoning-capable models fold much of that into the model's own internal reasoning — but the underlying idea still holds, and is worth seeing explicitly once. The core idea is to interleave reasoning and action in a repeating cycle:

1. The agent reasons about the current situation ("Thought").
2. It chooses and executes an action — typically a tool call.
3. It observes the result ("Observation").
4. It updates its reasoning and decides on the next step.
5. This thought–action–observation loop repeats until a stopping condition is met.

In pseudocode (adapted from the [smolagents documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/smolagents/conceptual_guides/intro_agents)):

```python
memory = [user_defined_task]

while llm_should_continue(memory):
    action = llm_get_next_action(memory)
    observations = execute_action(action)
    memory += [action, observations]

final_answer = llm_generate_answer(memory)
return final_answer
```
![Visualization of the ReAct agent loop (from [the n8n blog](https://blog.n8n.io/react-agent/))](../imgs/react-agent-n8n.jpg){width=60%}

The intelligence of the system is not in the loop itself — that part is trivial. It lies in three things:

- the **prompting** that shapes how the LLM reasons and selects actions,
- the **tool design** (signatures, descriptions, and error behavior), and
- the **memory representation** — what gets recorded, in what format, and subject to what limits.

Get those three right, and a surprisingly simple loop can produce remarkably capable behavior.


## Pipelines vs. agents – when do we need agency?

An agent is defined by its ability to decide. This brings flexibility – but also complexity and potential instability. You have to decide, if an agent is necessary to solve your problem or if you are better off using a pipeline.
Actually, most of the examples you find in tutorials will be better solved with a pipeline. We will use the example from the [smolagents introduction](https://huggingface.co/docs/smolagents/conceptual_guides/intro_agents) to illustrate that.


Let’s take an example: say you’re making an app that handles customer requests on a surfing trip website. Consider these two scenarios:

__1. Simple, predictable workflow__

You know in advance that user requests fall into a few categories and can be handled by a fixed sequence of steps.

- If the user wants general information on surf trips → show a search interface over your FAQ.
- If the user wants to talk to sales → collect their contact details in a form.

Here, a hand-coded workflow is simpler, more robust, and easier to test.

__2. Open-ended, complex workflow__
Let's assume the user asks:

“I can come on Monday, but I forgot my passport so I might be delayed to Wednesday. Is it possible to take me and my luggage surfing on Tuesday morning, with cancellation insurance?”

This touches several aspects (availability, logistics, insurance) where a fixed decision tree might become unwieldy. An agent can interpret the request and decide which information and tools are needed.

__Rule of thumb:__

If your workflow is essentially “always do A, then B, then C”, a pipeline of LLM calls (plus classic code) is often enough. If you regularly need adaptive decisions, an agent becomes attractive.

For RAG-style systems, this is particularly relevant:

- If retrieval is mandatory for correctness, you may not want to leave the “call retrieval or not?” decision to the LLM.
- Instead, you enforce: “always retrieve, then generate”, implemented as a pipeline.

::: {.callout-note}
## 📝 Task

Discuss: for the examples encountered so far, does it make sense to use an agent? Or would a pipeline be sufficient? Maybe even better?

:::


## Frameworks

Implementing all of this from scratch is instructive, but quickly becomes involved. In practice, you would reach for a framework — and there is no shortage of options. Here is a non-exhaustive overview: 

- [**smolagents**](https://huggingface.co/docs/smolagents/index): A lightweight agent framework by Hugging Face, designed to be simple and hackable. It has good conceptual documentation and an active community, making it a natural starting point.
- [**LlamaIndex**](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index): Originally a data framework for building LLM applications around your own data. It has grown to offer convenient abstractions for tools, agents, and memory, with many examples and tutorials.
- [**Haystack**](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack): An open-source NLP framework focused on production-ready applications, developed by the German company deepset. It supports both LLMs and classical NLP models.
- [**LangChain**](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain): A modular library for building LLM applications — chains, agents, tools — with a large ecosystem of integrations. One of the most widely adopted frameworks in the space.
- [**LangGraph**](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/overview): An agent framework by the LangChain team that models agent behavior as a graph of states and transitions, giving you finer control over multi-step workflows.
- [**n8n**](https://n8n.io/): A low-code/no-code platform for workflow automation, useful when you want to wire together tools and APIs without writing much code.
- [**Agent Development Kit (ADK)**](https://adk.dev): Google's agent framework, introduced in 2025 and now actively developed across Python, Java, Go, and Kotlin SDKs. It comes with strong tooling and production-oriented design.

For a quick prototype or to get a feel for agent mechanics, smolagents is a good choice — it stays close to the concepts without too much abstraction. In this course, we build hands-on with the ADK, introduced next.


## Google ADK: first contact {#sec-adk-intro}

Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) is a Python framework for building multi-agent systems with explicit graph-topology primitives [@erwinhuizengaAgentDevelopmentKit2025]. Its main advantage for teaching is the built-in Dev UI, which renders the agent graph and execution trace in a browser with zero configuration. Comparable frameworks you may encounter include LangGraph (more granular node-based control), CrewAI (role-based agent teams), and AutoGen (conversation-based multi-agent coordination). ADK sits at the structured and illustrative end of this spectrum.

ADK does not speak to Ollama or LM Studio directly. It requires a LiteLlm wrapper that translates between ADK's interface and the local provider's API. LiteLlm is a thin SDK adapter, not a running service. The model string must include a provider prefix that tells LiteLLM which backend to use:

```Bash
uv add google-adk litellm
```

```Python
from google.adk.models.lite_llm import LiteLlm
import os

# Ollama
os.environ["OLLAMA_API_BASE"] = "http://localhost:11434"
model = LiteLlm(model="ollama_chat/gemma3:latest")

# LM Studio
os.environ["LM_STUDIO_API_BASE"] = "http://localhost:1234"
model = LiteLlm(model="lm_studio/gemma3")
```

Without the prefix LiteLLM cannot route the request and raises a BadRequestError. The prefix is the only required change when switching backends.

The three types needed for first contact are LlmAgent, Runner, and Session. An LlmAgent is a leaf node: a single LLM call with a system prompt and optional tools. Runner executes a pipeline against a Session, which holds conversation and pipeline state. ADK has further composition types, introduced in @sec-orchestration once we actually need them.

| Type | Role |
|---|---|
| LlmAgent | Leaf node: one LLM call, one system prompt |
| FunctionNode | Leaf node: a Python function as a graph step |
| Workflow | Graph of nodes connected by explicit edges; handles sequential, looping, and parallel topologies |
| Runner | Executes a pipeline against a session |
| Session | Holds conversation and pipeline state |

Full API reference: [https://google.github.io/adk-docs/](https://google.github.io/adk-docs/)



::: {.callout-note}
## 📝 Task

1. Install the dependencies: ``uv add google-adk litellm``
2. Make sure Ollama is running with a model that supports tool calls (e.g. ``gemma3``, ``qwen3:8b``, ``llama3:instruct``).
3. Write a minimal agent: an ``LlmAgent`` wired up to your local model via ``LiteLlm``, run through a ``Runner`` against a ``Session``, with one message sent to confirm it responds.
4. Start the Dev UI: ``adk web`` and explore the agent tree in the browser.

:::

:::{#tip-adk_hello .callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
### Example: a minimal ADK agent

```Python
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.adk.models.lite_llm import LiteLlm
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.genai import types
import os

os.environ["OLLAMA_API_BASE"] = "http://localhost:11434"

agent = LlmAgent(
    name="Hello",
    model=LiteLlm(model="ollama_chat/gemma3:latest"),
    instruction="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
)

session_service = InMemorySessionService()
runner = Runner(agent=agent, app_name="hello", session_service=session_service)
session = session_service.create_session_sync(app_name="hello", user_id="student")

for event in runner.run(
    user_id="student",
    session_id=session.id,
    new_message=types.Content(role="user", parts=[types.Part(text="Say hello!")])
):
    if event.is_final_response():
        print(event.content.parts[0].text)
```
:::

Right now we have an agent with no tools — is it really an agent at all? Time to give it something to do, closing the loop back to @sec-functioncalling.

::: {.callout-note}
## 📝 Task

1. Define the weather tool — a **read-only** tool, in the terms we introduced earlier — as a plain Python function with type hints and a docstring. ADK derives the tool's schema from these automatically, no hand-written JSON schema required.
2. Now define a second tool that actually *does* something — an **action** tool this time: one that creates or overwrites a text file in a local folder.
3. Pass both tools to your agent via ``tools=[get_current_weather, write_note]`` when constructing the ``LlmAgent``.
4. Ask the agent something that should trigger each tool in turn (e.g. "What's the weather in Berlin? Also, jot that down in a file called weather.txt.") and confirm, in the Dev UI's trace or the printed events, that both tools were actually called.
5. Compare this to the two ways of wiring up a tool call from @sec-functioncalling: what does ADK still do for you, and what would you have had to write by hand without it?
6. Before you run it: think about what could go wrong with an action tool that can overwrite any file the agent decides to name, with no confirmation step. What would you want in place before handing an agent a tool like this for real, beyond "it's just a demo"?

:::

:::{#tip-adk_tools .callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
### Example: a read-only and an action tool

```Python
def get_current_weather(location: str, unit: str = "celsius") -> dict:
    """Get the current weather in a given location.

    Args:
        location: City name.
        unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit".

    Returns:
        A dict describing the (mocked) current weather.
    """
    return {"location": location, "unit": unit, "forecast": "sunny", "temperature": 21}


def write_note(filename: str, content: str) -> dict:
    """Create or overwrite a text file in the local 'notes' folder.

    Args:
        filename: Name of the file to write, e.g. "todo.txt".
        content: Text content to write into the file.

    Returns:
        A dict confirming the file path that was written.
    """
    import os
    os.makedirs("notes", exist_ok=True)
    path = os.path.join("notes", filename)
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        f.write(content)
    return {"path": path}
```
:::


## Model context protocol

You just wrote the `get_current_weather` and `write_note` tools yourself, by hand, as plain Python functions. That works fine for a couple of tools you own — but what if you want your agent to use a tool someone else already built, or you want to expose a tool you wrote so that *other* people's agents can use it too, without everyone inventing their own calling convention? In a company setting this comes up constantly: an agent that's supposed to gather information from the ERP system, look up tickets in Jira, or search an internal wiki needs some way to reach all of those systems that isn't "someone hand-writes a bespoke Python wrapper for each one."

Before a standard existed, this meant a custom, one-off integration for every tool/model combination — a different key for every door. The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** standardizes this: a common way for a host application to discover and call tools exposed by any server, instead of one-off integration code per tool source. Anthropic defined the protocol and released reference implementations in several languages (including Python), plus a growing ecosystem of pre-built servers for third-party services — so you don't have to write, or re-write, an integration from scratch every time your agent needs to reach a new system.

::: {.callout-note}
## 📝 Task

Before getting into how MCP works, see it in action.

1. Install the [MCP Inspector](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/tools/inspector): ``npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector``
2. Connect it to the reference [filesystem server](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/filesystem) (the Inspector's own quickstart shows the exact command for your platform).
3. Browse the tools, resources, and prompts it exposes, and try calling one of its tools directly from the Inspector UI.

:::

But what is an MCP server anyway? And how does MCP work exactly?


### Core concepts

The Inspector you just used *is* an MCP **Host** — here's the fuller picture of what it was talking to. At its core, MCP follows a client-server architecture where a host application can connect to multiple servers:

![MCP architecture [@ModelContextProtocol]](../imgs/MCP_archi.png)


- **MCP Hosts:** Programs like Claude Desktop, IDEs, or AI tools that want to access data through MCP
- **MCP Clients:** Protocol clients that maintain 1:1 connections with servers
- **MCP Servers:** Lightweight programs that each expose specific capabilities through the standardized Model Context Protocol
- **Local Data Sources:** Your computer’s files, databases, and services that MCP servers can securely access
- **Remote Services:** External systems available over the internet (e.g., through APIs) that MCP servers can connect to

The servers come in three main flavours:

- **Resources:** File-like data that can be read by clients (like API responses or file contents)
- **Tools:** Functions that can be called by the LLM (with user approval)
- **Prompts:** Pre-written templates that help users accomplish specific tasks

This course focuses on Tools, since that's what an agent calls directly — Resources and Prompts matter more once you're building a full MCP host, which is beyond what we cover here.

::: {.callout-note}

2. Connect your ADK agent to the same filesystem MCP server from the Inspector task, instead of your hand-written `write_note` function.
3. Ask it to do something that writes or edits a file, and confirm it goes through the MCP server this time.
4. Compare: what did you get for free by using the MCP server instead of your own function? What did you lose (e.g. control over exactly what the tool does)?

:::

## Wrap-up

We started this session already holding every piece an agent needs — tool definitions, parsing, execution, feeding results back — because all of that was built in @sec-functioncalling. The only genuinely new ingredient today was control: instead of a human (or a hard-coded pipeline) deciding what happens next, the model itself decides, inside a loop that keeps calling it until it's done.

That reframes most of what we did as harness again, not model capability: ReAct is just a convention for *how* the loop talks to itself, ADK is a framework that implements the loop (plus a graph of nodes) so you don't have to, and MCP is a standard for *where tools come from* so you're not stuck hand-writing every integration. None of it changes what the model can do in a single turn — it changes how many turns it gets, and how much of the world it can reach from inside them. That reach is also why today's ADK task gave the agent a real **action** tool, not just a read-only one: the moment a tool can actually change something, a bad decision in the loop stops being just a bad answer.

The judgment call that matters most going forward isn't "can I build an agent for this" — usually yes — but "should I": a fixed pipeline is simpler, cheaper, and easier to debug whenever the steps are known in advance, and agency is worth its added complexity only once they aren't.

Next session, we scale this up: instead of one agent deciding everything, multiple agents coordinate on a larger task.
